approved: Treasury Laws Amendment (OECD Multilateral Instrument) Bill 2018

The Labor member moved a second reading amendment noting the Coalition's failure to close multinational tax loopholes and improve tax haven transparency, while supporting the bill to implement the OECD multilateral convention. Labor also criticised the government for claiming credit for tax measures it had previously opposed and outlined its own plan to tighten tax transparency, close loopholes, and crack down on tax havens.

The speaker argued the Turnbull government has failed to curb multinational tax avoidance, noting one in five of Australia's biggest companies paid no tax in three years and that Goldman Sachs paid zero tax on $1.8 billion revenue, while the government rejected key anti-avoidance articles 10 and 12 of the OECD multilateral instrument. They proposed Labor's alternative policies, including public country-by-country reporting, closing debt deduction loopholes (adding $5.4 billion over a decade), introducing a beneficial ownership registry, and rewarding whistleblowers.

The speaker supported the amendment to the Treasury Laws Amendment Bill, noting the government declined to adopt articles 10 and 12 of the OECD convention targeting tax havens. A future Shorten Labor government would review that decision and, if elected, require large extractive companies to disclose payments on a country-by-country and project-by-project basis from 2020.

The government argued its anti-avoidance laws have raised $7 billion in tax liabilities and collected $4.1 billion, including $1 billion from ecommerce companies, while Labor opposed these measures. The bill will modify 31 of Australia's 44 bilateral tax treaties to align with international best practice on curbing multinational tax avoidance.
